blocks.title: The atom
blocks.md: An atom has a tiny, dense **nucleus** of **protons** (+1) and **neutrons** (0) with **electrons** (−1) orbiting it. The **proton number Z** = number of protons (= number of electrons in a neutral atom); the **nucleon number A** = protons + neutrons. Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons are **isotopes** (e.g. carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons).

blocks.title: Radioactivity
blocks.md:
Some unstable nuclei **decay** by themselves (spontaneously and randomly), emitting radiation:

- **Alpha (α)**: a helium nucleus (2 protons + 2 neutrons); strongly ionising; stopped by paper or a few cm of air.
- **Beta (β)**: a fast electron from the nucleus; stopped by a few mm of aluminium.
- **Gamma (γ)**: electromagnetic radiation; weakly ionising, very penetrating; reduced by thick lead or concrete.

blocks.title: Decay changes
blocks.md:
- **Alpha decay**: A decreases by 4 and Z by 2.
- **Beta decay**: A is unchanged and Z increases by 1 (a neutron becomes a proton).
- **Gamma emission**: no change in A or Z.

Radiation is detected with a **Geiger-Müller tube** and counter. **Background radiation** (from rocks, space, buildings) must be subtracted from readings.

blocks.title: Safety and watch out
blocks.md: Radiation can damage cells. Sources are handled with **tongs**, kept in **lead-lined containers**, at a distance, and for as short a time as possible. Do not confuse **radioactive** with **hot**: radioactive decay is not affected by temperature or chemical state.

blocks.caption: Penetrating power of alpha, beta and gamma radiation.
blocks.alt: A radioactive source with three arrows: alpha stopped by a thin sheet of paper, beta stopped by aluminium and gamma stopped only by thick lead.

blocks.title: Example 1 — alpha decay
blocks.statement: Uranium-238 (Z = 92) emits an alpha particle. Find the nucleon number and the proton number of the new nucleus.
steps: Alpha decay: A decreases by 4 and Z by 2.
New A = 238 − 4 = 234 and new Z = 92 − 2 = 90, which is thorium-234 (Z = 90).

blocks.title: Example 2 — beta decay
blocks.statement: Carbon-14 (Z = 6) is a beta emitter. Find the new nucleus.
steps: Beta decay: A stays 14 and Z increases by 1 to 7.
Z = 7 is nitrogen, so the product is nitrogen-14.

blocks.title: Half-life
blocks.md: The **half-life** of a radioactive isotope is the time for **half** of the nuclei in a sample to decay (equivalently, for the **count rate** to fall to half). Half-lives range from fractions of a second to billions of years. It is unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical changes.

blocks.title: Calculating
blocks.md:
After n half-lives the fraction left is $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n$. Method:
1. Find the number of half-lives n = total time ÷ half-life.
2. Halve the amount n times.
3. For count rates, subtract the **background** first.

blocks.title: Uses
blocks.md:
- **Medicine**: gamma rays kill cancer cells and sterilise equipment; short half-life tracers show how organs work.
- **Industry**: gauges that control the thickness of sheets; finding leaks in pipes.
- **Dating**: carbon-14 estimates the age of ancient wood and bones.
- **Smoke detectors**: use a small alpha source.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.md:
- Half-life does **not** mean the sample is all gone after two half-lives: half of a half remains (a quarter).
- Use the same units for time and half-life.
- Choose short half-life sources for medical tracers (so they disappear quickly from the body).

blocks.caption: Decay curve of a sample whose half-life is 3 days: the mass halves every 3 days.
blocks.alt: A falling exponential curve starting at 80 g, passing 40 g at 3 days, 20 g at 6 days and 10 g at 9 days.
